scope: Primary sources for biological gas secretion, retention and barrier crystals, verified on 2026-10-09; goldbeater's skin is in envelope_sources.json.

sources.citation: Scholander, P. F. and van Dam, L. (1954). Secretion of gases against high pressures in the swimbladder of deep sea fishes. I. Oxygen dissociation in blood. Biological Bulletin 107(2), 247-259.
sources.access: Full text (Biodiversity Heritage Library OCR) read by a verification agent.
sources.use: Oxygen pressures commonly above 100 atm; swim-bladder fish to at least 266 atm; nitrogen 2-15% of the oxygen; fish from 320-1,300 m; summarises Jacobs (1930) on the rete retaining gas despite circulation.
sources.limit: Their conclusion that the Root effect is not the mechanism was later replaced; not cited for mechanism.

sources.citation: Scholander, P. F. (1954). Secretion of gases against high pressures in the swimbladder of deep sea fishes. II. The rete mirabile. Biological Bulletin 107(2), 260-277.
sources.access: Full text (BHL OCR) read by a verification agent.
sources.use: Rete capillaries 7-13 mm in deep-sea species, more than 1 cm in some, lengthening generally with depth; the wall must be very impermeable, with crystals and/or fibres.

sources.citation: Kuhn, W., Ramel, A., Kuhn, H. J. and Marti, E. (1963). The filling mechanism of the swimbladder. Generation of high gas pressures through hairpin countercurrent multiplication. Experientia 19, 497-511.
sources.use: Countercurrent multiplication of a single concentrating effect.

sources.citation: Pelster, B. (2015). Swimbladder function and the spawning migration of the European eel Anguilla anguilla. Frontiers in Physiology 5, 486.
sources.access: Open-access full text read by a verification agent.
sources.use: Gas-gland cells turn about 80% of glucose taken up into lactate; CO2 from the pentose phosphate shunt; acidification switches on the Root effect; salting-out; countercurrent multiplication by back-diffusion from venous to arterial rete capillaries.

sources.citation: Pelster, B. (2023). Journal of Comparative Physiology B 193, 307-313.
sources.access: Introduction read by a verification agent.
sources.use: Eel rete: about 58,000 arterial and 44,000 venous capillaries, 1-2 um apart, over a few millimetres; PO2 and PCO2 rise 7-8-fold.

sources.citation: Lapennas, G. N. and Schmidt-Nielsen, K. (1977). Swimbladder permeability to oxygen. Journal of Experimental Biology 67(1), 175-196.
sources.use: Low O2 conductance lies in the submucosa, from a low diffusion coefficient caused by multiple layers of very thin (about 0.02 um) and broad (up to 100 um) crystals, presumably guanine, occupying a small fraction of tissue volume.

sources.citation: Denton, E. J., Liddicoat, J. D. and Taylor, D. W. (1972). Journal of the Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom 52(3), 727-746 (title not recorded here).
sources.access: Abstract read by a verification agent.
sources.use: Intact wall far less permeable to CO2, O2 and N2 than connective tissue; removing the silvery guanine layer increases permeability about 100 times; two deep-sea eels carry about 10 times the guanine per unit area of the conger eel.
sources.limit: Permeability of the deep-sea eels not measured.

sources.citation: Wittenberg, J. B., Copeland, D. E., Haedrich, R. L. and Child, J. S. (1980). Journal of the Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom 60, 263-276 ("... The swimbladder wall is a lipid-rich barrier to oxygen diffusion").
sources.access: Abstract read by a verification agent.
sources.use: Oxygen pressure difference across the wall close to 300 atm at 3,000 m.
sources.limit: Lipid barrier view beside the guanine view.

sources.citation: Pinsk, N. et al. (2022). Journal of the American Chemical Society 144(11), 5180-5189.
sources.access: Open-access full text read by a verification agent.
sources.use: Sardine swim-bladder guanine plates 2-50 um wide and under 20 nm thick; the swim bladder's silvery guanine layer serves as a gas diffusion barrier.

sources.citation: Nielsen, L. E. (1967). Models for the permeability of filled polymer systems. Journal of Macromolecular Science: Part A - Chemistry 1(5), 929-942.
sources.access: Record only; formula checked in Idris, Muntean and Mesic (2022), Journal of Coatings Technology and Research 19(3), 699-716, doi:10.1007/s11998-021-00579-6 (open access, read by a verification agent).
sources.use: P/P0 = (1 - phi)/(1 + (L/2W) phi), with L/W the platelets' length over thickness.
sources.limit: Aligned, separated, evenly dispersed plates normal to diffusion.

sources.citation: Wittenberg, J. B. (1960). The source of carbon monoxide in the float of the Portuguese man-of-war, Physalia physalis L. Journal of Experimental Biology 37(4), 698-705.
sources.access: Summary read by a verification agent.
sources.use: Carbon monoxide 0.5-13% of float gas, oxygen 15-20%, CO2 negligible; the gas gland (pneumadena) forms CO from L-serine; large folic acid concentration; CO later replaced by air through diffusion and exchange.
sources.limit: Nitrogen and argon not given in the summary.

sources.citation: Dunn, C. W. and Wagner, G. P. (2006). The evolution of colony-level development in the Siphonophora (Cnidaria: Hydrozoa). Development Genes and Evolution 216(12), 743-754.
sources.access: Full text (author PDF) read by a verification agent.
sources.use: Colonies of zooids homologous to solitary animals: pneumatophore, nectophores, gastrozooids, palpons, gonophores on gonodendra, bracts; probuds arise in growth zones that also lengthen the stem; Physalia is a cystonect without a long stem.

sources.citation: Sander, R. Compilation of Henry's law constants (version 4.0, Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics 15, 4399-4981, 2015; online at henrys-law.org).
sources.access: Online entry for hydrogen read on 2026-10-09.
sources.use: H2 solubility 7.7-7.8e-6 mol m-3 Pa-1 at 298.15 K across literature reviews and measurements (e.g. Fernandez-Prini et al. 2003, 7.8e-6).
